sentences.text: Aeolosaurus was a large, long-necked, quadrupedal herbivore measuring around 14 meters in length.
The type species A. rionegrinus had a robust build with limb bones similar in strength to Saltasaurus, whereas A. maximus appears to have been more slender.

Aeolosaurus is diagnosed by distinctive tail vertebrae featuring downward-curving prezygapophyses in anterior vertebrae and chevrons with concave posterodorsal surfaces containing double anterior articular facets.
The osteoderms of Aeolosaurus were unusual, with most resembling those of Mendozasaurus, and associated osteoderms provide evidence that this dinosaur was armored.
Estimates for the animal's size vary significantly, with Gregory S. Paul estimating it at 6 tonnes while Molina-Pérez and Larramendi suggested it could reach 14.7 tonnes.

The third species, A. maximus, is the largest known member of the genus and is known from an incomplete skeleton including cervical, dorsal, and tail vertebrae, ribs, and appendicular elements found in the Adamantina Formation, Brazil.
The genus and type species Aeolosaurus rionegrinus were named and described by Jaime Powell in 1987.
The type species was discovered in the Angostura Colorada Formation in Argentina, dating from 83 to 74 million years ago.

The holotype of Aeolosaurus rionegrinus includes seven tail vertebrae and parts of the forelimbs and right hindlimb, specifically a series of seven vertebrae with most of both hind limbs and the right forelimb.
The name Aeolosaurus honors the Greek mythological figure Aeolus due to the frequent winds in Patagonia where fossils were found.
A second species, Aeolosaurus colhuehuapensis, was named in 2007 from Patagonia by Casal et al.
A third species, Aeolosaurus maximus, was named in 2011.

Aeolosaurus shared its Late Cretaceous environment with hadrosaurs, and an unnamed Aeolosaurus species from the Allen Formation lived alongside five other titanosaur species, hadrosaurs, and ankylosaurs.
The unnamed Allen Formation species shared its environment with five other titanosaur species, including Rocasaurus muniozi, as well as hadrosaurs and ankylosaurs.
In 2004, Aeolosaurus and Gondwanatitan were grouped together in the clade Aeolosaurini, a grouping established by Franco-Costa et al. to include Aeolosaurus rionegrinus and Gondwanatitan faustoi.
In 2016, Franca et al. placed Aeolosaurus and its relatives in the family Aeolosauridae as the sister taxon to Saltasauridae within the superfamily Saltasauroidea.

There are currently two valid named species of Aeolosaurus, plus several unnamed specimens, and scientists have not formally named two possible new Aeolosaurus species due to the genus being poorly known.
Aeolosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically during the late Cretaceous Campanian stage, approximately 74 to 70 million years ago, in what is now South America.
Aeolosaurus lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.

Aeolosaurus fossils are found across South America during the Late Cretaceous, having been collected from formations in Argentina and Brazil, making it a widespread genus of titanosaurs known from the late Cretaceous of South America.

Because the genus Aeolosaurus is not well known, authors chose not to formally name potential new species, even though Gondwanatitan faustoi, the closest known relative, has been proposed to represent an additional Aeolosaurus species, but Gondwanatitan is normally considered a distinct genus.
